## One layer: 4 nodes → 3 nodes

Take two consecutive layers: layer 1 has 4 nodes and layer 2 has 3. Layer 1's
nodes output $f(a_{1,1}), \dots, f(a_{1,4})$ — their pre-activations $a_{1,i}$ passed
through an activation function $f$. Every layer-1 node connects to every layer-2
node, and each connection carries one weight:

> $w_{j,i}$ is the weight on the edge **into** layer-2 node $j$ **from** layer-1
> node $i$.

So there are $4 \times 3 = 12$ weights. (In my handwritten notes I tagged the first
couple of weights with a superscript, $w^{(a_2)}_{1,1}$, to say which layer they
feed. Within a single layer that tag is the same for every weight, so I drop it
here; with several layers I'd write $W^{(2)}, W^{(3)}, \dots$ instead.)

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-network-2d >}}

Each layer-2 node simply adds up its incoming edges — each layer-1 output scaled
by its weight:

$$
a_{2,j} = \sum_{i=1}^{4} w_{j,i}\, f(a_{1,i}), \qquad j = 1, 2, 3.
$$

The same graph in 3D, with each layer in its own plane, makes the **fully
connected** structure obvious: every node in one plane talks to every node in the
next. All edges into one layer-2 node share a color — those are exactly the
weights $w_{j,1}, \dots, w_{j,4}$ in that node's sum.

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-network-3d >}}

## The matrix view

Stacking the weights so that **row $j$ holds all the weights into node $j$** turns
the three sums into one matrix–vector product:

$$
W = \begin{bmatrix}
w_{1,1} & w_{1,2} & w_{1,3} & w_{1,4} \\
w_{2,1} & w_{2,2} & w_{2,3} & w_{2,4} \\
w_{3,1} & w_{3,2} & w_{3,3} & w_{3,4}
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\boxed{\;\underbrace{\mathbf{a}_2}_{3\times1} = \underbrace{W}_{3\times4}\;\underbrace{f(\mathbf{a}_1)}_{4\times1}\;}
$$

This is why the index order is **destination first, source second**: row $j$ of
$W$ dotted with $f(\mathbf{a}_1)$ is exactly the sum for node $j$. The matrix has one
row per node in the *next* layer and one column per node in the *previous* layer.
In the notebook I compute $\mathbf{a}_2$ both ways — looping over the 12 edges and
using `W @ f(a1)` — and they agree.

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-weight-matrix >}}

::: {.callout-note title="What my notes leave out: the bias"}
In practice each node also adds a bias, so the layer is
$\mathbf{a}_2 = W f(\mathbf{a}_1) + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
As in [logistic regression](../../logistic-regression/two-class-linear/index.qmd)
(where $w_0$ multiplies a constant feature $1$), the bias can be folded into $W$ by
adding a 5th layer-1 "node" that always outputs $1$ and making $\mathbf{b}$ a 5th
column of $W$.
:::

## Forward propagation through many layers

A deeper network just repeats this step. With the input $\mathbf{x}$ playing the
role of layer 0's output,

$$
\mathbf{a}^{(1)} = W^{(1)} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}, \qquad
\mathbf{a}^{(l)} = W^{(l)} f\big(\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)}\big) + \mathbf{b}^{(l)}, \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \sigma\big(\mathbf{a}^{(L)}\big),
$$

where the last layer uses softmax $\sigma$ (below) for classification. *Forward
propagation* is just evaluating this chain from input to output: alternate a
linear map (the weights) with an element-wise non-linearity (the activation).

## Activation functions

Why bother with $f$ at all? Without it, two layers give
$W^{(2)}\big(W^{(1)}\mathbf{x}\big) = \big(W^{(2)}W^{(1)}\big)\mathbf{x}$ — a single
linear map, so depth would add nothing. The activation is what makes a network
**non-linear**. It is applied **element-wise**, one node at a time.

| Name | $f(x)$ | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Sigmoid | $\sigma(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$ | output in $(0, 1)$; saturates at both ends |
| Tanh | $\tanh x = \dfrac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}$ | output in $(-1, 1)$; zero-centered |
| Linear | $kx$ | no non-linearity (used at regression outputs) |
| Step | $1$ if $x \ge 0$, else $0$ | the classic perceptron; zero gradient |
| Saturating linear ("logic threshold") | $\min\!\big(\max(x, -L), L\big)$ | linear in the middle, flat beyond $\pm L$ |
| ReLU | $\max(0, x)$ | the modern default for hidden layers |
| Leaky ReLU | $x$ if $x \ge 0$, else $c\,x$ | small slope $c$ (e.g. $0.01$) for $x<0$ |
| ELU | $x$ if $x \ge 0$, else $\alpha\,(e^{x}-1)$ | smooth; tends to $-\alpha$ (often $\alpha = 1$) |
| GELU | $x\,\Phi(x)$, $\;\Phi(x) = \tfrac12\big(1+\operatorname{erf}(x/\sqrt2)\big)$ | smooth ReLU; used in Transformers |

A few clarifications on what I wrote by hand:

- **Step:** my sketch put the jump a little right of center. The jump is at
  $x = 0$; a threshold $\theta$ (which the bias provides) shifts it to $x = \theta$.
- **Logic threshold:** I sketched it without a formula, flat at $-4$ and $4$ with
  a ramp in between, so I've written it as the saturating linear function with
  $L = 4$. I'm not sure the $\pm4$ is standard — the common version, *hard tanh*,
  uses $L = 1$.
- **GELU:** $\Phi$ is the standard normal **CDF** (capital $\Phi$; I wrote a
  lowercase $\phi$, which usually means the density).

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-activations >}}

The dashed curves are the derivatives, which training (backpropagation) relies on:

- **Sigmoid and tanh flatten out** away from 0, so their derivatives vanish there
  — through many layers this causes *vanishing gradients*.
- **Step has zero derivative** everywhere it's defined, so gradient descent gets
  no signal through it; the saturating linear function has the same problem once
  it saturates.
- **ReLU** keeps a slope of 1 for $x > 0$ but is exactly flat for $x < 0$ (a node
  stuck there stops learning). **Leaky ReLU**, **ELU**, and **GELU** all keep some
  signal for $x < 0$.

## Softmax for classification

For a classifier with $k$ classes, the output layer uses **softmax**:

$$
\sigma(\mathbf{a})_i = \frac{e^{a_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k} e^{a_j}}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, k.
$$

(I wrote this formula twice in my notes, once as the "classification softmax
function" and once as the "softmax activation function" — it's the same function.)

- **Outputs are positive and sum to 1**, so they can be viewed as class
  probabilities; the prediction is the class with the largest one.
- **Not element-wise:** unlike the activations above, each output depends on
  *all* the $a_j$ through the denominator.
- **Shift-invariant:** adding the same constant to every $a_i$ changes nothing
  ($e^{c}$ cancels), so implementations subtract $\max_j a_j$ first to avoid
  overflow.
- **Two classes reduce to the sigmoid:**
  $\sigma(\mathbf{a})_1 = \dfrac{e^{a_1}}{e^{a_1} + e^{a_2}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-(a_1 - a_2)}}$,
  which is the logistic-regression output.

{{< embed demo.ipynb#fig-softmax >}}
